entities.summary:
The Zhou dynasty (1046–256 BCE) was the longest-lasting dynasty in Chinese history, ruling for 790 years. Though weakening politically in its final centuries into the Warring States period, the Zhou era produced Confucius, Laozi, Sun Tzu, and Mencius — making it the most intellectually fertile period in Chinese history and the source of Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism, and Mohism in the Hundred Schools of Thought.

The Western Zhou (1046-771 BCE) established the feudal system that decentralized power to regional lords in exchange for loyalty. When nomads sacked the capital Hao in 771 BCE, the Eastern Zhou period began, which despite political weakness produced the Chinese philosophical golden age. The Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BCE) saw the rise of Confucius (551-479 BCE), whose ethical teachings about proper relationships, benevolent governance, and self-cultivation became the foundation of Chinese civilization and East Asian culture broadly.

The Warring States period (475-221 BCE) saw seven competing kingdoms develop competing philosophies and innovative military and administrative techniques. Sun Tzu's 'The Art of War,' written during this era, remains the most widely read strategic text in military history. Iron smelting, cavalry warfare, and bureaucratic administration innovations during the Zhou period laid the technical and institutional foundations that the Qin dynasty unified under one rule.
